P1k: In every community there was somebody who took the initiative to get it started. Somebody found the land, wrote the first documents, taught the method, recruited the first members, or kept things going when everybody else lost interest.
P3k: I know this personally. Many of the methods discussed in this article were my doing, and I wrote the materials, so it would be very easy for me to become the person who decides whether or not everyone else “understood” them correctly. Writing in an anti-authoritarian way does not keep the author from enjoying being an author.
P4k: A few things help keep that in check. One is to judge the method by results people can actually see. Are the members flourishing, and are they safe? Can conflicts get resolved? Can people disagree, leave, and later tell a different story about it? Are the kids doing well once they grow up? Is the community still materially viable? Can it correct a prediction that turned out wrong? Can it replace the founder? And if it's meant to spread, do new projects actually start up and last? How long a community has lasted, how full it is, whether it reaches consensus and how many members stay aren't enough on their own. A group can keep its members because people love it, or because leaving costs too much. And don't judge it by how closely people stick to the founder's own interpretation.
P6k: Here are the four questions about the founder:
P7k: Can the community respectfully override the founder? Can the community replace the role of the founder? Can the community alter the vision of the founder? Can the community exist without the founder?
P8k: Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who's in charge of the housing and the food stores, the vehicles and tools, and any bank account outside the community? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the reviewers? Who controls access to the kids, or to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart might look flat and horizontal, while the keys, passwords, titles and general reputation all point to one person.
P9k: Remember, it's not an override unless it can actually work on the person in question. If the founder selects the person to review the founder, holds the records, has title to the land, and can kick out complainers, then there's no way for the community to override the founder, no matter how many circles it holds.
P11k: Also watch for the daily signs. Increasing focus on the founder over time. Sense that disagreement is failure. Every bad result is blamed on lack of good implementation. Increasing “insider” knowledge while public accountability decreases. Results are never measured. Sense that former members become morally contaminated the moment they leave.
P14n: “Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become compulsory disclosure, where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. A group starts out inviting honesty and ends up treating privacy as resistance.
P15k: Peer counseling can become peer surveillance, even if the tone is warm. And when there are pre-reqs for people to get medicine, they can put power in the hands of gatekeepers, right when people are at their most open. Even something couched in words like “willing to be seen” could become a demand that people disclose whatever the group wants them to.
P16k: The boundary is simple. These principles aren't things that give the community power over me, they're commitments I choose for my own practice.
P18k: The medicine is optional. Choosing not to take the medicine in no way affects anyone's rights as a member. The power to let people into the group doesn't sit with any individual or permanent clique. And disagreement has to be answered as disagreement.
P19k: “Your resistance is your wound talking” is pretty much a conversation ender. Once you notice a community diagnosing dissent like this instead of answering it, leave before they schedule a group process about your leaving.
P20k: There are some basics that the majority cannot vote away from any member of a community. These basics are your bodily safety, adequate food and sleep, the right to go to a doctor of your choice, the right to keep your thoughts private, the right to communicate with people outside the community, a way to report harm without asking the accused person's friends for permission, and a usable way to leave. Removing these from a community member is not consensual, even if a majority vote does it.
